summary: States requirements for a mechanism that identifies which name server instance answered a DNS query. With anycast and load balancing, many servers can share one address, making it hard to tell which one replied. A standard way to find out would help administrators with diagnostics. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When several DNS servers share one address, you cannot tell which one answered your question. RFC 4892 describes the trick used today to find out, explains why that trick is not good enough, and lists what a proper mechanism would have to do.

sections.title: Why It Is Hard to Tell Which Server Answered
sections.content:
Identifying which name server is responding to queries is often useful, particularly when trying to diagnose name server difficulties. This is most obviously useful for authoritative nameservers, in the attempt to diagnose the source or prevalence of inaccurate data, but it can also be useful for caching resolvers in similar and other situations. The ability has become more useful as DNS has become more critical to more Internet users and as network and server deployment topologies have become more complex.

The conventional means for determining which of several possible servers is answering has traditionally been the use of the server's IP address as a unique identifier. The modern Internet, though, has seen the deployment of load balancing, fault-tolerance and attack-resistance schemes such as the shared use of unicast IP addresses documented in RFC 3258. An unfortunate side effect is that using IP addresses as identifiers for DNS service has become problematic. Specifically, multiple dedicated DNS queries may not go to the same server even though sent to the same IP address, and non-DNS methods such as ICMP ping, TCP connections or non-DNS UDP packets, of the kind generated by tools like traceroute, may be even less certain to reach the same server as the one which received the DNS queries.

There is a well-known and frequently used technique for determining an identity for a nameserver more specific than the possibly non-unique server that answered the query sent to a given address. The widespread use of that convention suggests a need for a documented, interoperable means of querying the identity of a nameserver that may be part of an anycast or load-balancing cluster. At the same time, the convention has drawbacks that argue against standardising it as it has been practised.
sections.plainLanguage: When several servers answer at one address, the address no longer identifies the server. Asking the server directly is more reliable than probing it from outside, because the probe may reach a different machine in the pool.

sections.title: The Existing BIND Convention
sections.content:
The commonly deployed Berkeley Internet Name Domain implementation of the DNS protocol suite has supported a way of identifying a particular server for some time, using a standards-compliant if somewhat unusual DNS query. A query to a recent BIND server for a TXT resource record in class 3, CHAOS, for the domain name HOSTNAME.BIND. returns a string that the administrator can configure to give a unique identifier for the responding server. The value defaults to the result of a gethostname() call. The mechanism extends the BIND convention of using CHAOS class TXT resource record queries to sub-domains of the BIND domain for version information, and it has been copied by several name server vendors. A refinement drops the implementation-specific label and replaces BIND. with SERVER., so the query may appear as ID.SERVER..

For reference, the other well-known name used by recent versions of BIND within the CHAOS class is VERSION.BIND.. A query for a CHAOS TXT resource record for this name returns an administratively defined string which defaults to the software version of the server responding, though this is not generally implemented by other vendors.

The convention has four valuable attributes. It is within the DNS protocol itself, so an identification mechanism that relies on DNS is more likely to go to the same system as a normal DNS query, although that is not guaranteed. Because the identity information is requested and returned within DNS, it does not require allowing any other query mechanism to the server, such as holes in firewalls for otherwise disallowed ICMP Echo requests, so it is likely to reach the same server over a path subject to the same routing, resource and security policy, without special exceptions. It is simple to configure, because an administrator can easily turn it on and control the results. And it gives the administrator complete control over what information is given out, minimising passive leakage of implementation or configuration details that infrastructure operators often consider sensitive.

There are also serious drawbacks. It requires an additional query to correlate the answer to a DNS query under normal conditions with the supposed identity of the server that received the query, and there are many situations in which that simply is not reliable. It reserves an entire DNS class for what amounts to one zone, and while the CHAOS class is defined in RFC 1034 and RFC 1035, it is not clear that supporting it solely for this purpose is a good use of the namespace or of implementation effort. The original form, using BIND., is implementation specific, and BIND is only one DNS implementation, though at the time of writing it was probably the most prevalent for authoritative servers, which does not justify standardising its ad hoc solution to a problem shared across many operators and implementors; the refinement changes the query label but preserves the ad hoc mechanism. There is no convention or shared understanding of what information such an answer could or should contain, including a possible encoding or authentication mechanism. And although DNSSEC has been defined to cover all DNS classes, so that the TXT resource records returned could be signed, DNSSEC deployment for the CHAOS class is neither existent nor foreseeable, and since the answer is expected to be unique per server, signing it would be impossible in practice.
sections.plainLanguage: The trick in use today is to ask the server for a special text record that names it. It works because it stays inside DNS, so it reaches the same machine and needs no firewall exceptions. But it needs a second query to correlate with the first, it uses up a whole DNS class for one small job, and it is tied to one implementation's naming.

sections.title: What a Better Mechanism Must Do
sections.content:
The discussion of advantages and disadvantages suggests some requirements for a better solution, summarised as guidelines for any effort to provide appropriate protocol extensions.

First, the mechanism must be in-band for the DNS protocol, so the query for the server's identifying information can be part of a normal, operational query. It should also permit a separate, dedicated query for the same information, and it should preserve the ability of the CHAOS class TXT mechanism to work through firewalls and in other situations where only DNS can be relied upon to reach the server of interest.

Second, the new mechanism should not require dedicated namespaces or other reserved values outside the existing protocol mechanisms for these, that is, the OPT pseudo-RR. In particular it should not propagate the existing drawback of requiring support for a class and top level domain in the authoritative server, or in the querying tool, to be useful.

Third, support for the identification functionality should be easy to implement and easy to enable. It must be easy to disable, and should lend itself to access controls on who can query for it.

Fourth, it should be possible to return a unique identifier for a server without requiring the exposure of information that may be non-public and considered sensitive by the operator, such as a hostname or unicast IP address maintained for administrative purposes.

Fifth, it should be possible to authenticate the received data by some mechanism analogous to those provided by DNSSEC. In this context the need could be met by including encryption options in the specification of a new mechanism.

Sixth, the identification mechanism should not be implementation specific.
sections.plainLanguage: A proper mechanism should travel inside ordinary DNS, avoid inventing new name spaces, be easy to switch on and off, give out an identifier without giving away anything private, let the receiver check that the identifier is genuine, and work the same on every server software.

sections.title: Security and the Cost of Identifying Servers
sections.content:
Providing identifying information about which server is responding to a particular query from a particular location in the Internet can be seen as information leakage and thus a security risk. This motivates the suggestion that a new mechanism allow the administrator to disable the functionality altogether or partially restrict the availability of the data. It also suggests that the server identification data should not be readily correlated with a hostname or unicast IP address that may be considered private to the operator's management infrastructure.

Propagation of protocol or service meta-data can sometimes expose the application to denial of service or other attacks. Since the DNS is a critically important infrastructure service for the production Internet, extra care needs to be taken against this risk by designers, implementors and operators of a new mechanism for server identification.

Both authentication and confidentiality of server identification data are potentially of interest to administrators, who may wish to make such data available and reliable to themselves and their chosen associates only. That constraint implies both an ability to authenticate it to themselves and to keep it private from arbitrary other parties, which leads to the fourth and fifth characteristics of an improved solution.
sections.plainLanguage: Saying which server answered is itself a small leak of information, so the operator needs to be able to turn the feature off or restrict it, and the identifier should not be easy to tie back to the server's internal address or name.

sections.title: Where the Protocol Extension Is Specified
sections.content:
This document proposes no specific IANA action. Protocol extensions, if any, that meet the requirements described are out of scope for it. A proposed extension, specified and adopted by the normal IETF process, is described in the DNS Name Server Identifier option work, including the relevant IANA action.

The technique for host identification documented here was initially implemented by Paul Vixie of the Internet Software Consortium in the Berkeley Internet Name Daemon package. The newest version of the requirements document takes a significantly different direction from previous versions, owing to discussion among contributors to the DNS operations working group and others.
sections.plainLanguage: The document deliberately stops short of defining the mechanism. It points to the DNS Name Server Identifier option as the separate piece of work where the actual extension is being specified and registered.

viz.caption: THE SIX CHARACTERISTICS OF A BETTER MECHANISM

items.title: In-band for DNS
items.text: The query for the server's identity must be able to be part of a normal, operational query, and a separate dedicated query must still be possible.

items.title: No dedicated namespaces
items.text: It should not need reserved values outside the existing protocol mechanisms, such as the OPT pseudo-RR, or a special class and top level domain in the server or the tool.

items.title: Easy to enable and disable
items.text: Support should be easy to implement and to enable, easy to disable, and open to access controls on who may query for it.

items.title: Unique without exposure
items.text: A unique identifier must be returnable without exposing a hostname or unicast IP address the operator considers sensitive.

items.title: Authenticatable
items.text: The received data should be authenticatable by a mechanism analogous to DNSSEC, and encryption options could meet that need.

items.title: Not implementation-specific
items.text: The mechanism should work the same whatever the server software.
